extracted.intended_audience: novelists, critics, and serious readers interested in the craft and form of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying a novel's subject and judging or creating a coherent form that serves that subject; includes criteria on unity, scope, viewpoint, character-role, and economy of material. Uses close analysis (e.g., War and Peace) as exemplars and anti-examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist’s eye for a subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist’s ability to find and recognize a fruitful subject (in a human being, situation, or turn of thought) is a cardinal gift; the process of discovery may be mysterious, but the subject once announced makes the author accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and protect the initial subject. The writer's 'eye' for a subject is decisive — cultivate attention to striking human situations or ideas. No practical exhortation will replace the gift, but once the subject is known the rest of the craft is available. Example: Tolstoy’s discovery of his central idea is privileged and sets the subsequent treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and unity of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject must be 'one and whole and irreducible' — a novel cannot take shape until it has a single supporting subject; it should be expressible succinctly (the essay suggests 'in ten words').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before shaping form, identify the book's central subject in a concise phrase. If you cannot put the novelist’s intention into a phrase, it is not ready to become a novel. Use the subject to decide what material belongs and what is extraneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must coincide with subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form is that which 'makes the most of its subject'—a well-made book is one in which subject and form coincide and are indistinguishable, where 'the form expresses all the matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the structure, sequence of scenes, and narrative techniques to realize and express the subject fully. If form and subject disagree, there will be superfluous or missing material; revise until the form exhausts the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel’s scale (space, population, length) must suit the subject; some subjects demand 'a big and various population' and generous room, while others may need a narrower horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the novel’s size and variety of characters to the demands of the subject. Do not assume length alone justifies breadth—choose a scope that allows representative truth without needless expansion. Example: the march-of-life theme requires ample population and room.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of multiple, ununified designs
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel should not inadvertently contain two distinct, incompatible structures or central themes (e.g., the essay diagnoses War and Peace as a confusion of 'the drama of youth and age' and 'the drama of a great historic collision').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all major threads and themes cohere toward a single centre; if multiple large themes are present, either integrate them consciously or separate them into different works. Watch for passages that belong to a different unifying idea and remove or rework them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a centre (unifying focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book must have a centre — a unifying focal idea or organizing principle — otherwise its general shape will fail to satisfy the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate or create a central organizing idea and make sure scenes and character arcs relate to it. If readers cannot name what the novel is about, the centre is weak or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of material — avoid wastefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Material should be used for the purpose of the subject; inclusion of unrelated or excessive matter is 'wasteful of its subject' and damages the story's impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut or reassign scenes, digressions, or expository passages that do not further the subject. Ask whether every chapter advances or illuminates the central subject; if not, revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of development
rubrics_metrics.description: The story must be given its full development; an incomplete development of the chosen subject leaves the novel unsatisfying even if it is large in size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace each major narrative arc to a fulfilling culmination appropriate to the subject. Large novels must still ensure each principal theme is sufficiently developed, not merely introduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and appropriateness of point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of presentation (narrator’s presence vs. characters’ consciousness) must be consistent and appropriate to the subject; random or casual changes of viewpoint weaken unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the novel will mainly present events through characters' inner lives or through the authorial narrator and stick to a coherent approach, or signal and justify intentional shifts. Example: Tolstoy alternates between effacement (characters’ experience) and an authoritative narrator; inconsistency there contributes to formal confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize authorial exposition and 'pamphleteering'
rubrics_metrics.description: Long argumentative or explanatory passages in the voice of the author (e.g., Tolstoy's 'interminable chapters of comment and explanation') interrupt fiction and can be a distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatization or indirect presentation over essayistic intrusion. If the authorial argument is necessary, integrate it sparingly and ensure it serves the fiction rather than subordinating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper grouping and composition of scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Related scenes and episodes should be grouped and composed so they form coherent cycles or sequences; disordered or fragmentary grouping leaves a theme broken and incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange episodes to build cumulative effect and logical progression; avoid scattering related material so that the reader must piece unrelated fragments together without guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indirect onlooker/POV to enhance effect
rubrics_metrics.description: At high moments, presenting events 'through the mind of an onlooker' (indirectness) increases impact; choosing an onlooker (Napoleon, Kutusov, a child) can borrow their consciousness's value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ indirect viewpoint strategically to intensify scenes, but choose onlookers consistently and purposefully rather than at random. Indirectness is a tool to be used for particular moments, not an ad hoc habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Abrupt, casual shifts (e.g., changes 'in the middle of a page') between themes or modes of narration teach the reader to expect disjunction and can erode coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark or prepare transitions between different narrative modes or themes so changes feel intentional. Smooth or signposted shifts preserve the reader’s sense of design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as representative of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be chosen and treated so that they embody or illustrate the novel’s central idea (e.g., Tolstoy’s young people as figures in the 'processional march of the generations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select character types whose lives and arcs clearly instantiate aspects of the subject. Decide whether characters will be shown as universal types or deeply particular historical figures and maintain that stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating a sense of world/space appropriate to the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel’s horizon (open, expansive or closed, concentrated) must fit the fable: some subjects require an 'ample vision' and continuity of life; others demand an intense, enclosed atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether to render an open, diffused world (as Tolstoy often does) or a confined, concentrated stage (as Dostoevsky does) according to the subject’s needs. Achieve the effect by proportioning description, cast size, and narrative reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on description to imply world
rubrics_metrics.description: A sense of freedom and broad world can be created without heavy descriptive passages; Tolstoy imparts vastness by freedom of characters rather than detailed description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey a wider world through character movement, social networks, and implications rather than dumping descriptive exposition. Use description selectively where it materially contributes to subject and form.
